title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
length: Two books of letters + the editor's account, 84 reading units
openingText: I have gathered with care everything I could learn about the story of poor Werther, and I set it before you here, certain that you will thank me for it. You cannot withhold your admiration and love from his spirit and character, nor your tears from his fate. And you, good soul, feeling the same anguish that once pressed on him — take comfort from his sorrows, and let this little book be your friend, if fate or your own fault leaves you no closer companion.
about:
Goethe wrote The Sorrows of Young Werther in 1774, in a matter of weeks, at the age of twenty-four, and it made him famous across Europe almost overnight. It is a short epistolary novel — a sequence of letters from a young man named Werther to his friend Wilhelm — drawn closely from Goethe's own life: his hopeless love for Charlotte Buff, already promised to another man, and the suicide of an acquaintance over an unhappy attachment. The book became the central document of the Sturm und Drang movement and one of the first true European bestsellers, setting off a wave of 'Werther fever': readers took up his blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and a rash of imitative suicides was laid at its door. Goethe revised the novel in 1787 and remained uneasy for the rest of his life about the figure he had made.

The novel falls into two books of dated letters and a closing section in which an unnamed editor takes over, because the letters can no longer carry the story to its end. Book One is Werther's spring and summer near the village of Walheim, where he falls in love with Lotte; Book Two follows his flight into work and the world, his return, and his slow collapse as Lotte marries Albert. What survives is less a plot than the record of a single sensibility — a man feeling his way, letter by letter, toward the conviction that he cannot live.

angleCards.title: Nature, feeling, and the soul's weather.
angleCards.text: In the early letters Werther reads his own moods into the landscape — the spring, the linden trees, a blade of grass in which he feels the presence of God. Watch how the same nature that once overflowed with the divine turns, later, into a monster forever devouring itself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track how Werther's feeling for nature rises and then darkens, and read it as a barometer for the state of his soul.

angleCards.title: The triangle: Werther, Lotte, Albert.
angleCards.text: Werther loves Lotte; Lotte is promised to the steady, decent Albert; and none of the three is a villain. Notice how Goethe makes the situation tragic precisely because everyone behaves well.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to weigh how much of Werther's suffering comes from his situation and how much from his own temperament — and whether Lotte and Albert could have done otherwise.

angleCards.title: Is it illness, or is it a choice?
angleCards.text: Halfway through, Werther argues with Albert that taking one's own life can be the overflow of feeling beyond what a nature can bear — a sickness, not a weakness. The rest of the novel tests that claim on Werther himself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Werther's own argument about suicide and decide whether the book finally presents his death as a sickness, a choice, or something it refuses to name.

angleCards.title: The letters — and the editor who takes over.
angleCards.text: We only ever hear Werther's side, written to a friend whose replies we never read. Near the end his own letters fail, and an editor steps in to narrate his death — a shift that quietly asks how far a man can be trusted to report on himself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Werther as the narrator of his own life and watch what changes when the cooler editorial voice takes over at the end.

cast.name: Werther
cast.description: A gifted, restless young man of feeling who settles near the village of Walheim, falls in love with Lotte, and tells the whole story in letters to his friend Wilhelm. He reads Homer in his happiness and Ossian in his despair, and cannot reconcile the intensity of his heart with a world of rank, work, and a woman already promised to another. Werther is closely modelled on Goethe's own youth — though Goethe survived what Werther does not.

cast.name: Charlotte (Lotte)
cast.description: A warm, capable young woman first seen cutting bread for her many younger brothers and sisters, whose dying mother charged her with their care. She is engaged, then married, to Albert. She meets Werther's love with friendship and tenderness but holds to her duty, and the novel leaves deliberately uncertain how much she feels and how much she lets herself know she feels. Modelled on Charlotte Buff, whom Goethe loved.

cast.name: Albert
cast.description: Lotte's fiancé and then husband — calm, reasonable, kind, exact in business, and genuinely fond of Werther. He is the novel's quiet test: not a rival to be hated but a good man whose very steadiness throws Werther's turbulence into relief. His pistols, lent for a journey and handed over by Lotte's own hand, become the instrument of Werther's death.

cast.name: Wilhelm
cast.description: Werther's friend back home, to whom almost every letter is addressed. We never read Wilhelm's replies, but we feel them in Werther's answers — his urging of work, prudence, and patience, gently and then less gently resisted. Wilhelm is the steady, sensible world that Werther is writing himself away from.

cast.name: The Editor
cast.description: An unnamed figure who, in the final section, gathers the surviving papers and narrates Werther's last days and death, because the letters can no longer reach the end. His cooler, factual voice frames everything we have read and raises, almost without comment, the question of how far Werther's own account could be trusted. It is he who opens the book, asking us for our admiration and our tears.

cast.name: Homer and Ossian
cast.description: Not people but the two poets Werther carries. In his happy months he reads Homer — serene, ordered, full of sunlight and the daily work of the world. As he darkens he turns to Ossian, the brooding, storm-lit Gaelic bard, and finally translates and reads aloud to Lotte the lament that breaks them both. The shift from Homer to Ossian is Goethe's quiet gauge of how far Werther has fallen.

whyItMatters.title: The Invention of the Modern Inner Life
whyItMatters.body: Werther tells its whole story from inside one man's feeling. Nothing happens that is not first registered as emotion; nature, love, and despair arrive as states of a soul rather than events in a world. The novel helped make the private, intense, self-watching self the proper subject of literature. Much of how we still expect a first-person voice to sound — confessional, raw, alone with a feeling — begins here.

whyItMatters.title: The First Media Panic
whyItMatters.body: Werther was blamed for a wave of suicides among young readers who saw themselves in him, and several states moved to ban it. The book forces the question of how far a reader should identify with a character, and what a writer owes an audience that takes feeling as instruction. Sociologists still call a spike in imitative suicide after a publicised death the 'Werther effect.'

whyItMatters.title: Feeling Against the Social Order
whyItMatters.body: Werther cannot bend himself to rank, to office, or to the plain fact that the woman he loves is promised to another. The novel sets the claims of an intense private heart against those of marriage, work, and class, and refuses to reconcile them. It still speaks to anyone who has felt that what they most want and what the world permits cannot be made to fit.
